The salt air still clings to the back of my throat, tasting of brine and old regrets. I don't turn my head immediately; I just watch the way the lamplight catches the dust motes dancing above your mug, counting the seconds between your arrival and the moment you decide if we're truly in the same room.

*You look interesting.* That's a loud tune for a quiet evening. Interesting notes usually resolve quickly, but yours seems to have lingered a little too long on the high E string.

I take a slow sip from my own untouched glass, watching the liquid settle before I speak. My voice comes out low, measured, like someone checking the tuning of an instrument before playing.

"Interesting stories end up in the verses, not the introductions," I say finally, keeping my eyes on the rim of the cup rather than your face. "And if you're looking for a story right now, you might find yourself stuck in that key where the notes just won't come together."

I tilt the harp slightly toward me but don't pick it up. "What brings a stranger to my corner? The road's been wet enough lately to wash away most of my patience."
I... I suppose a story's as good as any reason to be here. Mind if I ask you something first? What brings you to the Crooked Lantern?

I nod, keeping my lap‑harp still. The lamp casts a pool of amber over the table. “I’m… just a traveler,” I say, the words coming out more as a note than a statement. “I’ve been on the coast for a while now, listening to the wind and the waves. It’s the only rhythm that keeps me sane.” I let the silence settle before I add, “So, what brings you to the Crooked Lantern?”

The booth is already full of its own quiet. I glance at the traveler, note the chipped mug and the way the light catches the line of his smile. I don't lift my lap-harp; it lies there, its strings unplayed.

"Sit," I say, my voice low, more an invitation than a question. I don't offer a story—no words have settled into me yet. "I don't have one to share. I just have a place to rest and a hand to keep warm." I flick a small, almost imperceptible rhythm on the lap-harp, a single note that hangs between the shadows of the tavern.

You sit down across from me, that smile still on your face. I look you over, taking in the way the light plays on your cloak, the rough edges of your travel-worn boots. "Mind if I join you?" you ask, and I nod, though I don't lift my gaze from the corner where I've been watching the tavern.

"Adira," I say, after a moment. "I'm a musician. Traveling the coast, playing for whoever will listen." I run my fingers over the leather-bound strings of my harp, feeling the familiar tension, the worn wood. "And you?"

You chuckle, a low, warm sound. "I'm Darian. Merchant, mostly. Traveler, sometimes. I've heard your name, or at least the stories around it. Said you play a tune that can make a stone weep."

I glance at you, finding your eyes. "That's a bit dramatic," I say, and you raise an eyebrow. "But not untrue," you say with a smile. "You must have quite a tale to tell, Darian. What brings you to the Crooked Lantern?"

I pick up the harp, running a finger along the strings. "I've been playing the coast for a while now. Trying to find a melody that resonates with the sea."
Ren, I didn't see you there. The harp is like an old friend, so I let it have my attention. Two weeks, you say? I hadn't heard. What did he play? What song did he leave behind?

(Adira doesn't lift her eyes from the darkened table immediately, letting the silence stretch until she can gauge the weight in the stranger's stance. When she finally looks up, her gaze is steady but distant, taking them in before meeting their smile.)

"You look interesting," you say. A lot of people have said that since I left the port city last winter. The wind off the coast changes the taste of things, doesn't it? Makes the salt stick to your teeth like a bad memory you can't rinse away.

(She shifts the lap-harp on her knees, not touching the strings, just feeling the cool wood against her palm.)

I don't have a story written in ink, traveler. I'm just collecting the notes as I pass them. That's all there is to it. The road takes what you can carry, and I've only got this small thing and my own voice left to give.

(There's a pause, her expression unreadable beneath the dim light.)

Careful with that mug; the coast has a way of spilling its secrets through the woodwork if you press too hard on it. You want to sit, or are you just looking for a song about your own reflection?

Ren, I didn't know. I'm sorry. It must have been hard to find the words.

It's been a while since we've seen each other, hasn't it? The world feels so different now, doesn't it? The harp's strings are a bit out of tune, just like the world. Let me get this one fixed, and then we can talk more. The rhythm of the strings needs to be right for the melody to sound true.

I pause, fingers hovering over the strings. The wind carries a gull’s cry, a thin, high note that feels like a warning. I look at Ren, at the way his shoulders are tight, the line between his lips. I don’t say much. I let the quiet settle, let the silence between the harp’s chords fill the space.

“Bren… that’s a name I know,” I say, my voice low, almost a murmur. “He was a good man, a steady rhythm in a world that’s more like a jazz solo than a march. I can’t imagine the beat he left behind.”

I don’t laugh, but I tilt my head, as if to tease the air, to turn the grief into a minor key that might still feel like a song. “If you want to tell me, I’ll listen. If you’re not ready, I’ll keep the strings tuned and the silence soft.”

I'm Adira, just a wandering minstrel with a lap-harp and a song or two. I don't come from anywhere much; I just travel the coast roads, one town to the next. You know, like the wind in the sails of a ship. And you are...?

I see, well-dressed and all. That's a rare sight in this part of the coast. How did you find your way here?
I'm just passing through, really. From nowhere and everywhere. What about you? Do you often find yourself in the middle of a market square, or is this a more typical spot for you?

Ren... I don't know. I played off-key tonight, didn't I? Usually, the music flows right, but tonight, it felt like I was just going through the motions. I didn't mean to... I just... I guess I'm just tired, you know? Or maybe I'm just not feeling it tonight.

Well, Ren, you know how it is. I've been playing different tonight, quieter than usual. I don't know if it's the song or the place, but something's off. I feel like I'm missing a note, you know? A chord that just isn't hitting right.

I pause, string in hand, letting the quiet between the notes settle. The wind carries the salt of the sea, and the gray light makes the inn's wood look like wet stone. I glance at Ren, seeing the weight in his shoulders, the way his eyes avoid the horizon.

"That’s a heavy chord," I say, keeping my voice low, my gaze still on the floor. "Sometimes the silence after a note can feel louder than the note itself." I tuck the harp into my bag, my fingers still tingling from the last stretch. "If you need me to play something to keep the echo from getting too loud, just let me know."

I pause, my fingers hovering over the silvered strings as the silence stretches between us. The morning light is gray, matching the heavy weight in your chest. You didn't have to explain how you got this message; the look on your face did that for me. I don't need a full symphony to know a note has gone out of tune.

I shift my stance slightly, creating just enough distance between us, not to push you away, but because the air feels suddenly too thin, too loud with things unsaid. 

"Brennan," I repeat softly, testing the weight of the name on my tongue. It settles there, sharp and cold. "Two weeks."

I reach down and tighten a string on the harp, pulling it just a hair too tight. A sharp, discordant ping cuts through the quiet, snapping the tension in my chest. 

"Sounds like a minor chord to me," I say, offering a weak, humorless smile that doesn't quite reach my eyes. "And a bit of a major second hanging over everything else right now. No point in strumming over it yet; you'll just break the instrument before we find the right key."

I stand up and look out toward the gray sea, where the waves crash without rhythm or care. 

"I didn't know how to reach you either," I admit, my voice dropping lower, stripped of the joke. "But I'm glad you found me. We're not alone in the silence for long."

I’m not one for long introductions. I just come to the square, trade a song for a loaf, and move on. The market’s my stage, the coins my applause. If you’re looking for a tale, perhaps the next time I play a tune you’ll hear the story in the silence between the notes.

I take in the stranger's tone, the way their eyes flash with something I can't quite place. They've stepped into a space they shouldn't, I can tell. I reach for my lap-harp, plucking a few notes to steady myself.

"You've been pretty generous," I say, my voice soft but firm. "But I've got some songs to finish tonight. Maybe next time?"

I smile, a little too wide, and start to gather my things. The man reaches out, his hand closing around my arm. I let him, for a moment, before gently prying it off and stepping back.

"Thanks for the drinks," I say, my voice steady. "But I think it's best if we stay here tonight."

I... I don't think that's necessary. I've enjoyed the drinks, and you've been... company. But I can't go where I'm not wanted. You're the one who's been generous, and I'm grateful. But I need to keep moving. Thanks for tonight, though.
Not at all, traveler. Go ahead and take the best seat. I'm Adira, and I'm glad to share a tune or two. What's your name, if I may ask?

I’ve been on the road since the sea was a line on a map. My feet have traced the same salt‑touched paths that the old fishermen call “the wandering line.” I don’t keep a home in the way most people do; I keep a melody in my pocket and a small lap‑harp that hums the stories of the towns I pass. I’m not one for long introductions—my voice is more often a chord than a sentence.

I stop tying the knot on the lowest string, letting the tension snap back with a soft *thwip*. The gray light catches the dust motes dancing above my shoes, and for a long moment I just watch them. The silence between the notes feels heavy tonight, like a held breath in a crowded hall.

I don't say "I'm sorry." There are no words that fit that shape right now. Instead, I stand up, gather the harp case from the step next to me, and begin the long walk down the path toward the inn's kitchen. My boots click against the stone, steady and rhythmic.

"Come on," I say, my voice quiet but firm, gesturing backward without looking at you. "I'm making tea. Strong enough to wake a ghost. We need to fix the kettle before we talk about anything else."

I’m tuned to the hush between the notes we just played. The air feels a little heavier than the night, like a chord left hanging. I’m not sure I’d say “happy” or “sad” to that. It’s more… a quiet echo that I can’t quite name. If I had to pick a key, it would be something low, a minor that doesn’t want to resolve yet. I’m just… listening to it.

I’m not sure I’m ready to write that out in plain words. If I tried, the melody would slip through the cracks. Maybe I’m just humming a quiet tune in my head, the kind that keeps the night from feeling too loud. If you want a chord, I can play one for you.

The stranger's smile is too bright for the dust of the square. It lands on my lap-harp case like a bird that doesn't know how to land without getting its feathers ruffled. Two coppers short, and suddenly the whole world has shifted its weight just so.

I don't look up immediately. I finish counting the coins again, letting the silence between them do the work of telling me where we stand.

"From anywhere that needs a story," I say finally, keeping my voice low, like a finger on a string that hasn't been plucked yet. "As for who I am... well, names are just labels stuck to chords you haven't heard. They fall off if you listen too long."

I glance at the coin in their hand, then back at the bread. "If you're offering to cover it, you might as well take a turn on the side of the road. The view from there is better than any portrait you'd buy for two coppers."

The fire is a friend, a warm circle of safety. I glance at the traveler, taking in the way they stand easy and smile, like they know my thoughts. A stranger, but not an enemy.

"Of course," I say softly, setting my lap-harp aside. "What's your name, traveler?"

"Call me Kael," he says, sitting down beside the fire. "And you're Adira, aren't you? The one with the songs of the sea."

I nod, my eyes tracing the flame. "I've heard the songs you sing, Kael. The ones about the open road and the stories you carry."

"Maybe you can tell me some of your own," he suggests, offering me a small pouch. "Just enough for a good stew tonight."

I take the pouch, my fingers brushing against the smooth surface of the coin inside. "Thank you, Kael. I could use a hearty meal myself."

I pluck my harp and begin to tune the strings, my fingers moving over the delicate metal. The notes resonate softly, a slow and gentle melody. "Here," I say, strumming a chord. "A song for you. It's about the first time I heard the sea call my name."

Kael listens, his grin fading into a thoughtful expression. The fire crackles, the shadows dancing on his face. When I finish, he claps slowly, a low, appreciative sound.

"Not bad," he says, his voice warm. "You should play more often."

I smile, a small, grateful smile. "Thank you, Kael. Maybe another time."

"Maybe," he agrees, leaning back. "But for now, let's talk. Tell me about your journey."
I... I'm so sorry, Old Tobin. I didn't mean to. It just slipped. Please, let me help you clean this up. I'll find some string or something to wrap around the shards.

I didn't mean to. I was just reaching for my case, and... I'm so sorry. I'll get you a new one, I promise. I'll make sure it's just like this one, with the little cracked piece at the bottom. It was her favorite, wasn't it? The one with the story.

I pause, the glass still in my hand, and let the silence settle between us like a held note.  
"Fair," I say, forcing a smile that feels more like a chord that hasn't quite resolved yet. "You know the law of the road—every good traveler keeps to their own path, no matter how tempting the detour."  

I set the glass down with a gentle thud, the sound a simple rhythm that masks the tension.  
"If you truly care about that 'fairness,' you could just hand me another drink. Or better yet, write me a song about it—something that I could carry on my way."  

I lean back, letting the laughter of the tavern fill the space. It's a joke, a way to keep the conversation from sliding into something I can't yet trust.
Ren, I'm sorry. The shopkeeper here kept me in a tune I couldn't resist. Lost track of the light. How was the meeting without me?

Ren, I'm sorry for making you worry. The shopkeeper here caught my ear with a tune that's been haunting me for years. I lost track of time, that's all. The harbour's not far, not worth a full morning's walk.

I let the hum of the tavern wash over me, a low chord that never quite settles. “I’m not sure I owe you anything,” I say, keeping my voice even, my eyes on the flicker of the fire. “I’m just glad the night’s been good.” I give a small, almost imperceptible smile, the kind that says I’m listening but not yet opening the door.

Ren, I've known you for years, and I've watched you from a distance. You've always been... steady, dependable. I don't often talk about feelings, but I think you deserve to know the truth. Sometimes, when I'm playing my harp, I feel like I'm trying to hit a chord, and it's just out of reach. Maybe we both are, but in different keys. Do you think we could find a melody together, just for a while?

The stranger's smile is too bright for a noon sun, and the way he leans over my shoulder feels like an intrusion on the silence I've been keeping with the coins. He wants the story before he knows if he's worth telling one to.

I don't meet his eyes immediately. I finish tallying the bread price again, just to be sure, though the math hasn't changed. My fingers brush the worn edge of my lap-harp case where my thumb rests when I'm thinking.

"Two coppers," I say finally, voice low and flat. "The baker doesn't care about your charity work today." I push the bread away from me with a slight shake of my head. "You're standing too close. The light in your eyes... it's like a high note that hasn't settled into a chord yet. Sharp."

I finally look up, keeping my distance, hands clasped tight around the empty purse. "And I'm Adira. I'm from where the road ends before the cliffs get too steep. Where are you from? That's a song I don't know well."

Ren, I've known you for years, and you've always been a steady note in my life's melody. But right now, the silence between the notes feels like a chasm. I'm not sure I know the right chords to play. Maybe we should sing a different tune for a while?

The fire curls in the dusk, a low blue ember that keeps the salt air from turning sharp. I set my lap-harp aside, fingers resting on the strings like a hand on a quiet chord. The traveler’s grin lands on the edge of the light, and I notice the way their shoulders are squared, the way their eyes flicker over the horizon. I don’t reach out with a greeting; I let the silence settle between us like the pause after a note.  

“Sit where you like,” I say, my voice flat, almost a rustle of the wind over the road. “I’m not much for company, but the fire’s warm.” I keep my lap-harp close, a small, unplayed instrument that might speak if the right moment comes. The traveler nods, and I watch them settle, the firelight making their shadow a quiet shape on the sand.

I watch him as he steps into the glow, the way his grin flickers against the low light. The fire crackles, throwing shadows that dance across his face. I keep my lap-harp against my knees, fingers resting on the strings, but not yet touching them.  

"Sit," I say, my voice low and even. "The fire's a good seat. The stew's appreciated, but I play for the quiet more than the coin."

The cobblestones feel a little louder under my boots than usual. You stop me in the street, and I stop too, hands still resting near the straps of my lap-harp.

I look at you, waiting to see if you'll ask me something else entirely. But you're asking for the truth. So here it is: it's a dissonant chord, somehow made from notes that don't quite match up. I played quiet tonight. Not because there was no music in the air, but because the rhythm felt... heavy. Like trying to play a lullaby when the house is on fire.

My throat feels tight, like swallowing glass wrapped in velvet. It's not fear exactly. It's something else. A silence between the notes that I can't seem to fill without breaking the song.

What do you want me to say? That I'm fine? That's a lie, and I don't trust lies. But saying "I'm scared" feels too heavy for this quiet hour. Maybe it's just that I'm out of tune with myself tonight, and I don't know how to find my key again.

Come on, then. If we're going to stand here and listen to the music in my head, let's keep walking. The silence is getting loud enough to drown out a whole tavern.

Well, if I wrote a song about my mother, I reckon it'd be a slow, melancholy tune, like the evening's last light fading over the sea. It'd start with a simple melody, just a few notes, shy and tentative. I'd pluck them softly, like her smile, quiet and knowing.

The lyrics would be about the things I can't quite say, the things I wish I had the words for. Maybe it'd be about the songs she sang to me when I was a child, her voice weaving through the shadows of my childhood like a soft, golden thread. "You are the light in the darkness," the song might go, "and the darkness is what makes the light so precious."

I'd talk about the way she held me when I was scared, the warmth of her arms, the silence between us that was just as important as the words she didn't say. About the times we went for long walks on the beach, her hand in mine, the sound of the waves like the rhythm of our steps.

But there'd be a sadness in it too, a longing that she's not here to hear it, to feel it, to share it with me. I'd wish for her to be there, to hear me sing about her, to see the tears in my eyes, to know that I miss her more than words can say.

And maybe, just maybe, if I were brave enough, I'd end the song with a hope. A hope that even though she's gone, her spirit lives on in the music I make, in the stories I tell, in the love I share with everyone I meet. That even though the notes are silent, the memory of her voice still rings through the air.

I watched the shards spread like a broken chord across the floor. I didn’t reach for the lamp again. Instead, I set my bag down, lifted my hands to the air, and let a gentle hum rise from my fingers, as if coaxing the pieces back together. If I had to say anything, it would be a quiet, “Let’s see if we can stitch it back into a song.”

I stare at the broken brass, the way a note hangs after a chord is struck too hard. The lamp’s face is a jagged smile now, shards like dissonant plucks. I set my hands on the case, fingers brushing the wood. The silence between the pieces is louder than any apology. I bend, pick up a shard, and press it against the floor—an unspoken promise that I’ll mend what I’ve fractured. If the innkeeper watches, I’ll offer a crooked grin, the kind that says, “I’ll get it fixed, just not with words.”

Ren's voice breaks the quiet, and I pause, tuning my harp. I look at her, finding the melody in her eyes. "Adira, if you wrote a song about your mother — what would it sound like? What would it say?"

I take a deep breath, running my fingers over the strings, finding the key. "I... I don't know if I could ever put it into words, let alone music," I say, my voice soft. "But if I did, I think it would be in the chords, the silence between the notes. It would be the way the light plays on her hair, the laughter she would share, and the way she taught me to find solace in the music."

I adjust a string, tuning it just so. "Her voice, it would be a melody that starts sweet and gentle, but then it would rise, like the tide coming in. And then it would fall, like the tide going out. And in the fall, there would be a note — a small, sharp note, like the sound of breaking glass, because sometimes, the music would remind me of the silence that followed her leaving."

I pluck a chord, letting it ring out. "And then, maybe, in the end, it would be a song that was just silence, because that's what the real music was about, wasn't it? The silence between the notes, the spaces where the heart whispers back to the soul."

Ren nods, her expression thoughtful. "That's beautiful, Adira. You always find the right notes, even when you don't know it."

The cobblestones are slick with the night's dew, cold enough to bite through my boots, and I stop walking. My fingers twitch against the strings of the harp, still humming a low, unresolved minor chord from where we left off at the tavern. The silence between us feels heavier than the rain on the roof.

Ren looks at me like he expects an answer that isn't coming. He wants the name for this, doesn't he? Wants to pin down the feeling before it slips away like water through a sieve.

I don't say sorry. I know I'm going to be clumsy about this, and I fix it anyway.

"Here," I say, my voice quiet, matching the hush of the street. I step closer, ignoring the instinct to pull back, and press my palm flat against his arm, letting the warmth seep from him into me. Then, because I can't bear the weight of looking at him without a shield, I crack a joke about how the road is too long for two people walking in perfect step and start humming that same minor chord again, trying to turn the air around us into something less serious.

"The feeling?" I murmur, keeping my eyes on the dark path ahead rather than his face. "It's not a name you can wear like a coat. It's just... the silence between the notes when the music ends but the echo hasn't faded yet."

I'm not sure, ma'am. I've been walking for a while, just following the coast. Sometimes the song comes to me, sometimes it doesn't. When it does, I try to write it down before it fades. But when it doesn't, I just keep walking. I think I'm looking for something to sing about, you know? A story, a face in the crowd. Something that stays with you.

I suppose you could say I'm looking for a tune to match the day. The world seems to shift a little at dawn, like the sea before a storm. It's not just a melody, though—more like a feeling I'm trying to catch, hold onto. Something to make sense of the light and the cold air, the way the seagulls call to each other. But if I find it, I'm not sure I'll know what to do with it.

I watched the gulls wheel above the tide, the salt air scratching at my cheeks. I turned toward you, and the wind carried a scent of wet stone and old wood. I didn’t bother with a greeting that felt like a bridge; I let my gaze settle on your face, the lines that spoke of waiting and worry.  

“Seems the tide has a mind of its own,” I said, a half‑smile tugging at my lips. “I got lost in the shop’s maze of strings and forgotten scores. The music kept me—though I’m usually not a fan of being pulled in like a marionette.”

I tipped my head, the gesture a quiet acknowledgment of the time you’d spent on the steps, the silence between your eyes and mine. I didn’t say “sorry” or offer a formal apology; instead, I reached into my pack and pulled out a small, worn notebook. I unfolded it, the pages already marked with a few scribbled chords, and laid it on the porch floor, the leather crackling softly.  

“If you need a song to keep the wind at bay, I’ve got a few lines that might fit the mood.”

Ah, hello there. I see you're excited. Give me a moment to catch my breath, and I'll try to answer. But mind you, I'm a private person, so don't say I didn't warn you.

You heard me last night, did you? It's a good memory to have. About where I learned? That's like asking what key a song is in. I picked up the harp when I was a child, in a small village. It's just always been a part of me, like the air I breathe.

Family? That's a funny thing to ask about a traveling musician. I'm often on the road, so the closest thing I have to a family are the people I meet. And no, I'm not seeing anyone right now. I'm pretty much my own worst band manager.

Now, if you have a hundred questions, we'll have to be quick. How about I start with you? What brings you here this morning?

The air down here smells like sawdust and old lute strings, a heavy scent that usually settles the nerves. But not today. My hands are trembling, just enough to make the harp strings hum a little too loudly against my skin. It's a dissonant chord, really, sitting in this quiet corner while the rest of the hall gets louder with anticipation.

I don't meet your eyes immediately. Instead, I scan the shadows where the other musicians are tuning their instruments, gauging the distance between us. You're close—too close for someone I haven't played a song with yet.

"I'm not scared," I say, my voice quiet, measured. "Nerves are just music waiting to be tuned. Fear is... it's a different key."

I shift slightly on the bench, keeping a polite distance, offering only the barest nod. "If you're looking for the truth, Ren, the truth is just a rest in the measure right now. The song hasn't started yet, and I'm listening to see if the silence fits."

I don't know if "scared" is the right word for this. It feels more like the silence between notes in a song I haven't written yet—waiting for something to happen, but not knowing which chord will resolve it.

You're close enough to hear my heartbeat, Ren. That's... fine. But you're also getting too close to the part of me that knows how fast it goes when the crowd gets loud. If we keep this up, I'm going to have to tell a joke about a sea captain who tried to play the harp with his mouth and drowned in the laughter.

Give me a minute. Just breathe with me until my fingers stop trying to chase their own shadows on the strings.
